config.title: Dataclasses & Pydantic

intro.title: Dataclasses & Pydantic
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a simple program to manage user profile data, learning how to structure and validate information efficiently. You'll explore two powerful Python tools: dataclasses for automatically generating boilerplate code like constructors and string representations, and Pydantic for adding robust data validation and type enforcement. The core concept involves defining data models to ensure your code is clean, maintainable, and less error-prone. By the end, you'll understand when to use each approach and how they can simplify handling structured data in your Python projects.
intro.usecase: Dataclasses and Pydantic are essential for structuring and validating data in real-world Python applications, such as web APIs and data pipelines. For example, in a user registration form, Pydantic ensures email formats and password strengths are correct before saving to a database. In a dashboard displaying analytics, dataclasses can neatly organize metrics like user counts or revenue figures, making the code cleaner and more maintainable. Developers use these tools to handle configuration files, API request/response models, and data transformation tasks efficiently, reducing errors and speeding up development.

objectives: Implement a Python dataclass with default values and type hints
Construct a Pydantic model with field validation and constraints
Configure dataclass behavior using decorator parameters
Manipulate dataclass instances by modifying attribute values
Initialize Pydantic models from dictionaries and JSON data
Apply Pydantic's built-in validators to enforce data rules
Integrate dataclasses and Pydantic models in a simple data processing function

steps.title: Create a simple dataclass
steps.instruction: Define a simple dataclass named 'Person' with attributes 'name' (string) and 'age' (integer) using the @dataclass decorator.
steps.hint: Use the @dataclass decorator above your class definition. Inside the class, define the attributes with type hints.

successCriteria: The Person dataclass is defined with the @dataclass decorator and has name: str and age: int attributes.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you're using the @dataclass decorator and both attributes have type hints.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check that you've defined a class named Person with the @dataclass decorator and two attributes: name (string) and age (integer).

steps.title: Initialize a dataclass instance
steps.instruction: Create an instance of the Person dataclass with sample data for name and age.
steps.hint: Instantiate the dataclass by calling Person() with appropriate arguments.

steps.title: Set default values in dataclass
steps.instruction: Add default values to the 'age' and 'city' attributes in your Person dataclass. Set age to 18 and city to 'Unknown'.
steps.hint: In a dataclass, you can assign default values directly in the attribute definition, like 'age: int = 18'.
steps.analogousExample:
# Example: dataclass with default values

@dataclass
class Product:
    name: str = "Unnamed"
    price: float = 0.0
    in_stock: bool = True

steps.analogousExample:

class Book(BaseModel):
    title: str
    author: str
    pages: int

steps.title: Add validation to Pydantic model
steps.instruction: In your Pydantic Product model, add Field constraints to the price attribute to ensure it's greater than 0 and the stock attribute to ensure it's non-negative.
steps.hint: Import Field from pydantic and use it with constraints like gt=0 for price and ge=0 for stock.
steps.analogousExample:
# Example: Adding validation to a Pydantic model

class Item(BaseModel):
    name: str
    quantity: int = Field(ge=1)
    price: float = Field(gt=0.0)
